[MATERIALS AND METHODS]: Participants were adult Caucasians of both sexes and included 10,416 lean subjects with no MUS (Group A), 58,710 lean subjects with MUS (Group B) and 30,445 overweight/obese subjects with no MUS and excessive fat mass (FM) (Group C).

Title: Phase angle and cellular health: inflammation and oxidative damage.

Journal/Date: Reviews in endocrine & metabolic disorders (2023)

MeSH Keywords: Humans, Body Composition, Aging, Body Mass Index, Oxidative Stress, Inflammation


--- ABSTRACT ---
Phase angle is a composite measure that combines two raw bioelectrical impedance analysis measures: resistance and reactance. Phase angle has been considered an indicator of cellular health, integrity, and hydration. As inflammation and oxidative stress can damage cellular structures, phase angle has potential utility in early detecting inflammatory and oxidative status. Herein, we aimed to critically review the current understanding on the determinants of phase angle and its relationship with markers of inflammation and oxidative stress. We also discussed the potential role of phase angle in detecting chronic inflammation and related adverse outcomes. Several factors have been identified as predictors of phase angle, including age, sex, extracellular to intracellular water ratio, and fat-free mass. In addition to these factors, body mass index (BMI) also seems to influence phase angle. Available data also show that lower phase angle values are correlated (negligible to high correlation coefficients) with higher c-reactive protein, tumour necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6, and interleukin-10 in studies involving the general and aging populations, as well as patients with chronic conditions. Although fewer studies have evaluated the relationship between phase angle and markers of oxidative stress, available data also suggest that phase angle has potential to be used as an indicator (for screening) of oxidative damage. Future studies including diverse populations and bioelectrical impedance devices are required to confirm the validity and accuracy of phase angle as a marker of inflammation and oxidative stress for clinical use.

key_findings.finding: In a very large human multicentre cross-sectional study (n=99,571 adults), medically unexplained symptoms (used as a chronic stress/inflammation phenotype) were associated with higher extracellular water, lower intracellular water, and lower phase angle. Compared with lean asymptomatic participants, symptomatic lean participants had higher hs-CRP, a flattened/reversed salivary-cortisol rhythm (lower morning and higher evening cortisol), and lower phase angle. ECW correlated positively with hs-CRP and evening cortisol and negatively with morning cortisol; phase angle correlated positively with morning cortisol and negatively with evening cortisol and hs-CRP. The evidence is strong for association but not causality, and the study relied on a specific dual-frequency BIA device.

key_findings.finding: In 121 children/adolescents (ages 5–15), overweight/obesity was associated with higher state anxiety, fat mass and lower percent fat-free mass; percent fat mass correlated with hs-CRP (r=0.397, p=0.001), and serum hs-CRP correlated strongly with hair cortisol (r=0.777, p<0.001). The paper supports a stress–inflammation–adiposity relationship measured alongside BIA, but the available abstract does not establish a specific cortisol or psychological-stress association with phase angle, resistance, reactance, ECW or ICW.

source_tools.relevance: Direct pediatric human study with effect sizes and explicit limitation of the BIA-specific associations

key_findings.finding: A 2025 human cohort study (n=5,305; 1,654 normal-weight and 3,651 overweight/obese adults) found that phase angle and ECW/TBW were associated with hematological inflammatory markers, but patterns were not uniformly intuitive. Higher phase angle was associated with higher WBC in both BMI strata and with higher platelets/lymphocytes in overweight participants; higher ECW/TBW was associated with lower hemoglobin/hematocrit in both strata and with lower WBC in normal-weight participants, plus lower granulocytes/lymphocytes and inflammatory ratios in overweight participants. ECW/TBW showed stronger associations than phase angle, particularly in normal-weight individuals. This indicates BMI/context modification and that hematologic markers do not all track in the same direction.

source_tools.relevance: Direct large human BIA and hematology cohort with BMI-stratified directions

key_findings.finding: A review synthesizing human studies across general, aging, obesity, chronic kidney disease, COVID-19, ICU/hospitalized, psoriasis and other clinical populations reports that lower phase angle is generally associated with higher CRP, TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-10; reported correlations range from negligible to high. The review describes the direction as broadly consistent across studies, while emphasizing heterogeneity in populations, devices and designs and the need for validation before clinical use. Phase angle is derived from resistance and reactance, so the inflammatory association is primarily with their composite rather than with each raw parameter separately.

source_tools.relevance: Human evidence synthesis across multiple populations and inflammatory biomarkers

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: human evidence supports an association between stress/inflammation and bioimpedance, most consistently as greater fluid distribution toward ECW and lower phase angle with higher inflammatory burden or chronic-stress symptoms. Associations with cortisol are directionally coherent when diurnal timing is considered (higher evening/lower morning cortisol aligns with higher ECW and lower phase angle), whereas evidence for perceived stress, autonomic symptoms/HRV, leukocyte count and individual resistance/reactance values is sparse or context-dependent. Findings are not fully uniform across BMI and clinical populations, and most studies are cross-sectional or observational.
